title: Semi-device-independent quantum randomness certification in semiconductor spin-noise measurements
authors: Hamid Tebyanian, Marius Cizauskas, Manfred Bayer, Marc Assmann, Alex Greilich
abstract: Complex solid-state systems are promising platforms for scalable, high-bandwidth quantum random-number generation, yet certifying the quantum origin of their fluctuations remains difficult because the underlying microscopic dynamics are hard to model and validate. Here we demonstrate semi-device-independent quantum randomness certification from semiconductor spin noise, to our knowledge the first such certificate on any spin-noise source, without relying on a microscopic model of the spin system. The untrusted optical source is constrained by an experimentally tested mean-photon-number bound together with a declared analogue-range and per-sample clipping ceiling, while the trusted receiver is described as a calibrated, noisy, coarse-grained homodyne measurement. Using a semidefinite programme with rigorously controlled Fock-space truncation, we certify randomness that remains private against an adversary holding arbitrary quantum side information. Offline analysis yields certified entropy rates of $3.2$--$3.4$\,Gbit/s from a singly charged (In,Ga)As quantum-dot ensemble and $33$\,Mbit/s from $n$-GaAs in a spin-noise-matched detection mode. This exceeds the certified entropy rate of earlier spin-noise generators by more than two orders of magnitude, and the certificate tolerates a resolved per-symbol energy contribution from the solid-state emitter itself rather than requiring a near-vacuum input.
summary: This paper presents a novel semi-device-independent method to certify the quantum randomness generated by semiconductor spin noise. By applying semidefinite programming to the measured fluctuations, the authors establish high certified entropy rates for both quantum-dot and bulk GaAs systems. This work is significant because it provides a robust, model-free security guarantee for a scalable solid-state quantum random number generator.
main_problem: The core challenge is certifying the quantum origin of fluctuations for quantum random-number generation (QRNG) when using complex solid-state systems like semiconductor spin noise.
main_result: The authors achieved certified entropy rates of 3.2–3.4 Gbit/s from a quantum-dot ensemble and 33 Mbit/s from n-GaAs, significantly exceeding previous spin-noise generator rates.
method: They employ a semi-device-independent quantum randomness certification framework using a Semidefinite Programme (SDP) to bound the conditional min-entropy.
model_or_system: The physical platform is semiconductor spin noise measured via homodyne detection. The certification treats the source as untrusted, constrained only by an experimentally tested mean-photon-number bound, while the receiver is modeled as a calibrated, noisy measurement.
key_observables: Certified entropy rates (Gbit/s or Mbit/s), mean-photon-number bound ($ ar{n}$), and the conditional min-entropy ($h^*_{	ext{cert}}$).
important_parameters: The achieved rates (3.2–3.4 Gbit/s for QDs; 33 Mbit/s for n-GaAs), the energy bound $ ar{n}$, and the detection regimes (broadband vs. matched resonance).
main_assumptions: The certification relies on the source being constrained by an experimentally tested mean-photon-number bound, and the receiver is modeled as a calibrated POVM. The analysis uses Fock-space truncation and assumes IID effective modes in some analyses.
figures_summary: Figures summarize the certification architecture, compare different detection regimes (QD vs. GaAs), and show the dependence of entropy on binning and energy constraints.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of source certification in solid-state QRNG, details the semi-device-independent methodology using SDPs, presents the application to spin-noise measurements in both quantum-dot and bulk GaAs systems, and concludes with quantitative rate comparisons.
why_interesting: This work bridges quantum optics/information theory with solid-state physics by providing a rigorous, device-independent security proof for a practical quantum source, which is highly relevant for quantum networking and computation.

Figure 2: Experimental setup. A continuous-wave laser is split into a probe, which measures spin noise via Faraday rotation in the sample (held at 6 K in a transverse magnetic field Bx), and a local oscillator (LO) routed around the sample. The orthogonal-polarisation component after the sample interferes with the LO on a 50/50 non-polarizing beamsplitter (nPBS) and is detected by a balanced photoreceiver (BPR). The differential DC output drives the phase lock; the AC component is amplified, filtered, and digitized.
